topics: Data residency / private deployment vs hosted API
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-04 08:42 UTC
Duration: 48 min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Anya (Redwood CSM); Dr. Lena Ortiz, Rajiv Mehta, Simran Kaur, Tom Becker (HeliosGen)
---
00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you squeezing this in. quick rundwon of agenda — security pack, KMS, retention, and then any follow ups.
00:18 Dr. Lena Ortiz: thanks, Maya. big thing for us is we build clinical decision support workflows and so, uh, anything that touches PHI is — is, you know, sensitive. we need to be clear on whether customer content is used to train models or not.
00:32 Maya: absolutely. to be explicit, for our hosted offering we provide a "no-train" contractual commitment for customer data; we also have private/dedicated options where data never leaves the customer VPC. just to set expectations, our standard hosted api by default does not use customer inputs for future model training — that's in the docs — but we can also sign explicit language.
00:58 Simran: when you say "no-train" is that like a policy or is that technical isolation? like, how do you prove it?
01:06 Carlos: good question. technically we separate telemetry and telemetry used for model training. there is an ingestion pipeline we control, um, and there are flags on the request for ephemeral mode where we do not persist prompts beyond short TTL, and we don't route those payloads to the training buckets. there was a — sorry, there was a note about "kay em ess" integration which i'll get to.
01:32 Rajiv: can you explain the TTL and where logs end up? we have to make sure our SIEM isn't accidentally pulling PHI into long-term storage.
01:40 Maya: yeah. so for hosted api customers we retain full request payloads for up to 30 days by default for debugging and moderation, but those can be reduced or set to ephemerality at account level. for Dedicated we allow retention policies as low as 0 days (ephemeral) and customers can opt into log forwarding to their SIEM.
01:58 Tom: 30 days feels long for PHI, we want 0 by default. is that configurable for trial accounts?
02:05 Anya: it is configurable — the console has a retention control per route, and for pilots we can set the default to ephemeral. we'll follow up with a configuration guide.
02:14 Simran: ok. next — KMS. we need to ensure keys are customer-managed, rotate on our schedule, and never exported. how does Redwood support CMK and HSM-backed keys?
02:26 Carlos: we support Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) via standard kms integrations with major clouds. for Dedicated and Private, we support binding a CMK where encryption-at-rest and tokenization keys are wrapped by the CMK. HSM-backed keys — we have partners and can integrate via external HSMs; there's a small ops onboarding to set up a trust bundle. there is a doc, i'll send terraform snippets.
02:50 Rajiv: is that the same for model weights and cache? what parts are encrypted with the CMK?
02:58 Carlos: model weights live on disk in our serving nodes — for Private deployments those disks can be encrypted with your CMK; for Hosted, the control-plane can use our keys but customer data payloads are wrapped before persisting if you bind a CMK. note: we don't re-encrypt third-party open-model weights with customer keys in hosted offerings.
03:22 Dr. Lena: can you confirm that we can rotate keys on our cadence without downtime?
03:27 Carlos: yes, key rotation is supported with a double-write window — we stage new keys, rewrap objects on access, and the caller won't see downtime. rotation orchestration depends on the cloud provider; we have runbooks.
03:40 Maya: quick interjection — regulatory question: are you aiming for EU data residency?
03:44 Simran: yes, primary patient data must remain in eu-west-1 region.
03:49 Maya: good, we offer region pinning for both hosted and dedicated. for private on-prem, obviously you control residency.
03:55 Tom: audit logs — how long do audit trails last and can we ship them to our Splunk?
04:02 Carlos: audit logs can be exported to customer S3 or forwarded via syslog to your SIEM. retention is configurable; we typically keep syslog-forwarded logs for whatever the customer's retention policy is. we also keep internal audit chains for 12 months by default but can adjust for enterprise contracts.
04:22 Dr. Lena: we need immutability and tamper-evidence for audit trails for 7 years. is that supported?
04:29 Carlos: we can provide WORM-style storage in a customer-owned bucket and an append-only audit chain digest signed by our key. we'll need legal to sign off for long-term retention commitments, but technically feasible.
04:45 Rajiv: about SSO — we use SAML 2.0 and SCIM for provisioning. can Redwood integrate with our IdP and enforce RBAC per environment?
04:54 Maya: yes, SAML + SCIM supported and RBAC maps to roles you define. you can restrict access to models, routes, and billing. we also support just-in-time provisioning and SCIM group sync.
05:10 Simran: sometimes the transcriber ended up with "sammel" in earlier docs — sorry — but anyway. are there least-privilege defaults?
05:18 Anya: yes, least privilege is enforced for new accounts and can be hardened. we also provide an audit of permissions upon onboarding.
05:26 (Background: brief crosstalk)
05:40 Maya: ok let's deep-dive on the no-train contractual language — we offer two layers: contractual no-train (legal commitment) and technical opt-out flags. if you want a stronger guarantee we can do private deployment with zero telemetry leaving your network.
06:00 Dr. Lena: how do you prove no training was performed? what evidence can we see?
06:06 Carlos: we can provide logs showing data flow and the absence of writes to training buckets; we also have counters for the ingestion pipeline. those are redacted in public artifacts but we can provide customer-specific attestations. for an enterprise contract we'll include operational KPIs and a clause for audits.
06:28 Tom: for the pilot we need to simulate PHI ingestion but we want pseudonymization before it ever leaves our environment. any recommended patterns?
06:36 Carlos: best practice: you run a local pseudonymizer prior to sending, or use our SDK hook that masks identifying fields. we have regex-based and model-based scrubbers; model-based will sometimes have false positives/negatives so we usually recommend deterministic pseudonymization plus tokenization for IDs.
06:56 Rajiv: is there an option to run the scrubber in our VPC?
06:59 Carlos: yes, you can run the mask service in your VPC and call it before callouts. for Private deploys it's typical.
07:08 Simran: on the topic of prompt retention: do you keep embeddings separate? we do some analytics that rely on embeddings, and we can't have those persisted if they could reconstruct PHI.
07:18 Maya: embeddings are derived artifacts — by default they may be cached for performance but for enterprise we can disable embedding persistence or store them in your tenant-bound store wrapped by your CMK.
07:30 Dr. Lena: could embeddings be used to infer original text? we worry about reconstruction attacks.
07:36 Carlos: theoretically possible with small-ish corpora; that's why we recommend not persisting embeddings for PHI, or persisting them only in a customer-controlled encrypted store. we also support differential privacy options at request-level, though that has accuracy tradeoffs.
07:58 Simran: differential privacy — interesting. do you have any benchmarks on utility loss?
08:02 Carlos: yes we have internal evals; i'll attach a short note. generally epsilon settings under 1.0 start to impact accuracy noticeably for generation tasks.
08:12 (short pause)
08:25 Dr. Lena: ok let's cover legal — will Redwood sign a data processing agreement that includes no-training and subprocessors list?
08:32 Maya: yes, DPA with SOC2 and subprocessors list is standard. we will provide redacted SOC2 Type II at first then full on contracting.
08:40 Simran: do you do yearly pen tests and can we get reports?
08:46 Anya: redwood does annual third-party penetration tests; we can provide an exec summary and coordinate an on-site assessment if required under NDAs.
08:54 Rajiv: for the private deployment we might want to hook to our KMS using the HSM we already have. is there a recommended integration pattern?
08:59 Carlos: recommended is to expose a keystore endpoint in your VPC and use mutual TLS for the key-wrap operations. we support PKCS#11 bridges and some HSM vendors via partner connectors. there's a small operator runbook for the HSM trust establishment.
09:20 Tom: what's the expected timeline to stand up a private instance for a pilot?
09:24 Maya: usually 2-4 weeks for Dedicated and 4-8 weeks for on-prem private, depending on access and approvals. for pilot minimal config we can spin up a dedicated cluster in two weeks if you provide network peering and KMS creds.
09:36 Dr. Lena: about monitoring — we need full observability into inference calls, latency, and failure modes. can we get token-level logs minus the prompt content?
09:45 Carlos: yes, token-level telemetry (counts, latencies, errors) can be exported without payload. that's our recommended approach: export metrics and error traces while keeping content ephemeral.
09:58 Rajiv: what's the default SLA for Dedicated?
10:02 Maya: enterprise Dedicated SLA is 99.95% uptime for serving, with latency p95 targets in the contract. for pilot we'll not have a formal SLA but we'll instrument and agree on SLOs.
10:14 Simran: about export controls and recip— recipience? sorry. do you have any restrictions we should be aware of?
10:22 Maya: we comply with export control lists and sanctions screening for customers; if you operate in regulated countries we'll discuss.
10:30 (brief laughter)
10:36 Dr. Lena: ok, let's talk about deletion: suppose a user asks for erasure of their data — how quickly can you delete all associated artifacts including cache, KV, logs, embeddings?
10:46 Carlos: deletion request flows through our admin pipeline; for ephemeral mode deletion is immediate. for typical accounts with 30 day retention we purge after TTL. for enterprise with CMK binding we can also revoke keys making persisted ciphertext unreadable immediately while we run an object-pass to scrub indexes — but legal teams often want verifiable deletion logs. we can generate a deletion certificate.
11:14 Tom: the revocation approach is interesting. what's the risk that backups still contain plaintext?
11:19 Carlos: backups are encrypted; if you rotate/revoke a key we rewrap on restore windows. part of the onboarding involves ensuring backups are also under the CMK and subject to the same rotation.
11:32 Simran: back to audit — who can access logs internally at Redwood? is there separation of duties?
11:37 Anya: yes, we have RBAC and privileged access is audited. only ops-oncall and specific engineering roles can view raw payload logs and each access requires justification. we can provide a redacted access matrix.
11:52 Dr. Lena: will you permit a technical audit or pen test on a staging cluster that mimics our data flows?
11:58 Maya: yes, under NDA we can coordinate a scoped security assessment. we'll need to schedule and agree on the test plan.
12:08 Rajiv: ok, slightly tangential — what's the path to ensure model drift or regressions aren't introduced from your side? we want regression alerts if outputs degrade.
12:16 Carlos: we have eval hooks and can integrate your test prompts. Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals and trigger rollbacks if quality drops. results can be exported to your monitoring.
12:30 Simran: great. now practicalities for the pilot: we want to run a week-long pilot with pseudonymized PHI, KMS bound, logs shipped to our Splunk, and 0-day retention for request payloads. that sound feasible?
12:43 Maya: yes. proposed next steps: we'll send SOC2 & ISO artifacts; Carlos will send KMS how-to + terraform snippets; Tom will share rotation policy; then schedule a 60-minute infra deep dive next Wed.
12:58 Dr. Lena: add me to the deep dive please.
13:02 (Pause)
13:20 Maya: quick clarifying question — regarding the 0-day retention, do you still want exception storage for debug traces if errors occur?
13:28 Tom: we can accept ephemeral default with a 7-day debug window that requires explicit approval and is toggled only for reproducing incidents.
13:37 Carlos: we can implement a "debug jar" where traces are encrypted and require multi-party approval to access.
13:46 Simran: love that. one more: can you sign a clause that forbids training on our data, and include a right-to-audit?
13:56 Maya: yes, DPA + addendum can include explicit no-train and audit rights; legal will scope the audit frequency.
14:04 Dr. Lena: when you say audit, can we run a CSV of pipeline writes to confirm no writes to training buckets?
14:11 Carlos: yes, we can provide pipeline write logs and a digest; note some fields will be redacted but the write counts and destinations will be visible.
14:24 (Short silence)
14:32 Maya: other risk items?
14:34 Simran: data residency and key control — covered. also vendor subprocessors — will you share that list?
14:38 Anya: yes, we'll include the subprocessors list in the security pack.
14:43 Rajiv: and network connectivity — how is peering performed?
14:46 Maya: typically VPN or VPC peering depending on cloud, and we can use private link endpoints. security team will provide an access matrix.
14:55 Tom: for SIEM ingestion we'll want JSON schema for logs. can you deliver that?
15:00 Carlos: yes i'll include log schema and sample events in the doc bundle.
15:06 Dr. Lena: ok if you send everything by Friday we can review and get back with legal comments.
15:11 Maya: we'll aim for that.
15:14 (Crosstalk, agreement)
15:30 Maya: all right I'll do a quick recap of action items — Maya will send security artifacts including SOC2/ISO and subprocessors; Carlos will send KMS guide, HSM runbook, terraform; Tom to share rotation policy; we schedule deep dive next Wed. any objections?
15:48 Simran: none.
15:52 Dr. Lena: no.
15:55 Maya: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with the links.
16:02 (Meeting ends, short after-call chatter)
---
